title: Signature Consent Ledger
body:
The Signature Consent Ledger is an original design for keeping every health permission in one place that the patient can read at a glance. Each entry names the holder, the information covered, the recipients, the expiry, and how to withdraw, and entries are ordered by expiry so the permission that ends soonest is always on top. When a permission is withdrawn, the entry is marked closed but kept in the history, so the patient can later prove what was agreed and when it ended. The ledger is a design for a personal record, not a legal document, and it works alongside real consent forms rather than replacing them.

Method. The working method for this record is a ledger with five fields per entry and a monthly review. First, add an entry whenever a new permission is signed, copying the holder, scope, recipients, expiry, and withdrawal method exactly. Second, sort entries by expiry at each review. Third, mark entries that have expired or been withdrawn as closed, keeping them visible in history. Fourth, check that every open entry still matches a real need. Fifth, print or save the ledger before any major care change, so the new care team starts from an accurate list.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature consent ledger. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: lab expires 2026-06; clinic expires 2027-01; insurer expires 2027-06; soonest: lab Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a personal organization tool. It does not grant or withdraw legal permission by itself; real permissions change only through the holder's own process, which the ledger records. Do not store the ledger itself in an insecure shared location, because a list of all permissions is itself sensitive information.

title: Signature Sharing Dial
body:
The Signature Sharing Dial is an original design for setting how much health information flows to each recipient, using four positions instead of a single on-or-off switch. Position zero shares nothing. Position one shares appointment details only. Position two adds test results and messages. Position three adds the full record for a named care episode. The dial is set separately for each recipient, so a spouse, a caregiver, and a research project can each sit at a different position, and turning a dial down takes effect for future sharing while past sharing stays as it was.

Method. The working method for this record is a dial board with one dial per recipient. First, list every recipient. Second, set each dial to the lowest position that still allows the recipient's task. Third, review the board whenever a task changes, turning dials up or down as needed. Fourth, record each change with a date. Fifth, test the board by asking, for each recipient, what they could see today, and check the answer against the dial positions.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature sharing dial. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Signature Health Vault
body:
The Signature Health Vault is an original design for a personal store of health records that the patient controls, organized by episode rather than by provider. Each episode folder holds the visit notes, results, images, and bills for one course of care, with a cover sheet listing what is inside and where each item came from. The vault keeps an access log that records every time a folder is opened or copied, and the log itself is part of the vault, so the patient can see the history of their own records. The vault is a design for organization, not a medical record system, and it holds copies, leaving the provider's originals untouched.

Method. The working method for this record is an episode folder system. First, create one folder per episode of care with a cover sheet. Second, file each new item in the episode it belongs to, noting its source and date. Third, log every opening or copy in the access log. Fourth, review the log monthly and question any entry that is unfamiliar. Fifth, back up the vault in a second location the patient controls, and test that the backup can be opened.

title: Signature Permission Lantern
body:
The Signature Permission Lantern is an original design for making app permissions visible at a glance: each health app gets a lantern whose light shows how much it can access. A dim lantern means the app can access only what its job requires. A bright lantern means the app holds broad permissions, including ones unrelated to its job. The lantern brightens whenever an app gains a new permission after an update, so a quiet change in terms becomes a visible change in light. The patient reviews bright lanterns first, which turns an occasional audit into a quick daily glance.

Method. The working method for this record is a lantern board reviewed weekly. First, list every health app and its current permissions. Second, score each app by counting permissions unrelated to its job. Third, set each lantern's brightness from that count. Fourth, switch off unrelated permissions and watch the lantern dim. Fifth, remove apps whose lanterns stay bright after the audit, because broad permissions that survive review are a choice by the app, not an accident.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature permission lantern. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: step counter: 1 unrelated permissions; meal tracker: 3 unrelated permissions; sleep app: 0 unrelated permissions; symptom diary: 2 unrelated permissions; brightest: meal tracker Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a review habit, not as a security product: it shows permission counts, and it cannot show what an app actually did with data it already held. A dim lantern is a good sign, not a proof of good behavior, and a bright lantern is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict of wrongdoing.

title: Signature Caregiver Key
body:
The Signature Caregiver Key is an original design for giving a caregiver exactly the access their tasks need, in the form of a key cut for one door rather than a master key for the whole house. A driving key opens appointments only. A medicine key opens results and messaging. A billing key opens bills only. Keys are issued separately, expire separately, and can be taken back separately, so a caregiver who stops managing medicines keeps the driving key but loses the medicine key. The design keeps a key ring list that shows every key issued, to whom, for what, and until when.

Method. The working method for this record is a key ring with one key per task. First, list the caregiver's tasks. Second, cut one key per task at the matching level. Third, set an expiry on each key, even a distant one, so no key lasts forever by default. Fourth, review the ring when tasks change and collect keys that are no longer needed. Fifth, log every use the system records, and question uses that do not match the key's task.

title: Signature Identity Scrubber
body:
The Signature Identity Scrubber is an original teaching design for showing what de-identification removes and what it leaves behind. It takes a sample teaching record, lists every identifier type it contains, removes the listed types one by one, and then shows what remains: dates, places, or rare details that could still narrow identity. The scrubber scores the remaining record by counting leftover narrowing details, so learners can see that removing a name alone leaves a record that is still recognizable in context. The design uses invented teaching data only, never real patient records.

Method. The working method for this record is a scrub-and-score exercise. First, list the identifier types in the teaching record. Second, remove the listed types and print what remains. Third, count the narrowing details left behind, such as a rare diagnosis or a small town. Fourth, remove or generalize those details and score again. Fifth, compare the scores and state plainly what risk remains, rather than claiming the record is now anonymous.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature identity scrubber. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: fields: 4; after removing name, remaining: ['town', 'rare diagnosis', 'visit date']; narrowing details left: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design only as a teaching model with invented data. It is not a tool for de-identifying real health data, which requires trained staff, organizational rules, and review. Do not test the scrubber on real records, and do not describe a record as anonymous because a teaching exercise scored it low.

title: Signature Gene Locker
body:
The Signature Gene Locker is an original design for holding genetic information under separate locks for separate uses. One lock guards the raw data itself. A second lock guards research sharing. A third lock guards matching with other people. A fourth lock guards sharing with clinicians. Each lock is opened or closed independently, so a person can allow clinician sharing while keeping matching closed, or allow research sharing while keeping the raw data closed to download. The locker logs every opening, so the holder can see which lock was opened, when, and by whom.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-lock panel. First, name the four uses: raw data, research, matching, and clinician sharing. Second, set each lock from the person's actual wishes, not from defaults. Third, review the panel after any test, because new results can reopen questions that were settled for older results. Fourth, check the log regularly for openings that do not match the panel. Fifth, record family implications separately: a note that results can affect relatives, without copying the results into the note.

title: Signature Data Flow Map
body:
The Signature Data Flow Map is an original design for drawing the path health data takes from a device to every holder that receives it. Each holder is a station on the map, each transfer is a line, and each line is labeled with what travels on it and whether the patient can stop it. The map's value is that it makes hidden holders visible: a device that seems to talk only to a phone may in fact send data to a maker's servers and then to analytics partners, and the map shows all three stations. A flow that cannot be drawn because a policy hides a recipient is itself a finding, marked on the map as an unknown station.

Method. The working method for this record is a station-and-line drawing. First, list the device, the app, and the account. Second, add every recipient named in each holder's policy. Third, label each line with the data type and whether it can be switched off. Fourth, mark unknown recipients explicitly instead of omitting them. Fifth, re-draw the map after policy updates and compare the two drawings to spot new stations.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature data flow map. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1. watch; 2. phone app; 3. maker servers; 4. analytics partner; 5. unknown recipient; known stations: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a mapping habit for consumer devices and apps. It does not prove what a company did with data, only what its policies allow, and a complete-looking map is only as good as the policies it was drawn from. Where a policy is vague, the map should say so rather than guessing a clean flow.

title: Signature Form Filter
body:
The Signature Form Filter is an original design for answering health forms with only what the form's purpose requires. The filter reads each field, asks what purpose it serves, and sorts fields into three trays: needed, helpful, and unrelated. Needed fields are answered fully. Helpful fields are answered generally or supplied only to a named health professional. Unrelated fields are left blank with a polite question about why they are asked. The filter keeps a copy of the sorted form, so the person can later show exactly what was given and what was questioned.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-tray sort. First, read the form's stated purpose. Second, sort every field into a tray. Third, answer the needed tray completely and accurately. Fourth, handle the helpful tray with general answers or restricted delivery. Fifth, question the unrelated tray in writing and keep the question with the copy of the form.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature form filter. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: needed: 4; helpful: 2; unrelated: 3; fields total: 9 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a personal habit for school, work, and activity forms. It does not change legal requirements that may apply to particular programs, and it does not justify inventing information: a questioned field is left blank with a question, never filled with a false answer. When a form's purpose is genuinely unclear, asking the form's owner is part of the method, not a failure of it.

title: Signature Claims Window
body:
The Signature Claims Window is an original design for reviewing what an insurer sees, by showing the patient the same claim the insurer receives: diagnosis and procedure codes, dates, provider details, and amounts. The window highlights any code or date that does not match the care the patient remembers, and it keeps the explanation of benefits beside the claim so the two can be compared line by line. The design's point is transparency: a patient who can see the claim can ask precise questions about it, instead of disputing a bill in general terms.

Method. The working method for this record is a side-by-side review. First, place the claim and the explanation of benefits next to each other. Second, check every date, code, and amount against the care received. Third, highlight mismatches and write a question for each one. Fourth, send questions to the billing office in writing and keep copies. Fifth, file the reviewed claim with the bill so future questions start from an answered record.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. A mismatch is a question to ask, not proof of an error, and the billing office's answer belongs in the file with the claim.

title: Signature Breach Bell
body:
The Signature Breach Bell is an original design for responding to a breach notice without panic and without delay. When a notice arrives, the bell rings a five-step routine: file the notice, list the data types named, change affected credentials, watch statements for several months, and write down any question the notice leaves unanswered. The bell also sets a reminder bell for the months ahead, so the response does not end with the first week. The design treats the notice as the start of a task list, not as a verdict about harm, because a notice describes exposure, and harm depends on what happens next.

Method. The working method for this record is a dated bell log. First, record the notice and its arrival date. Second, list the data types it names. Third, change credentials for affected accounts and add a second sign-in step where offered. Fourth, set monthly statement reminders. Fifth, keep every later letter with the original notice. The log is reviewed at each reminder until the watch period ends, and then filed as a closed episode.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature breach bell. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1. notice filed; 2. data listed; 3. passwords changed; 4. reminders set; 5. questions written; log entries: 5 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as a personal response routine. It does not assess legal claims or compensation, and it does not replace the organization's own instructions in the notice. Do not trust unsolicited messages that claim to help with a breach and ask for passwords or payment; use the contact details in the original notice or on the organization's own website.

title: Signature Young Person's Data Room
body:
The Signature Young Person's Data Room is an original design for handing health data control from parent to young person in stages. The room has shelves for each holder of the young person's health information, and each shelf shows who consents, what is shared, and what the young person can already decide alone. As the young person grows, shelves move from the parent's side of the room to the young person's side, one shelf at a time, with a conversation at each move. The design does not set ages for the moves, because the ages at which young people control particular decisions vary by place and service; the family and the clinic fill in the local details together.

Method. The working method for this record is a staged shelf move. First, list every holder on its shelf. Second, mark each shelf as parent-managed, shared, or young-person-managed. Third, choose one shelf to move at each stage, and talk through what changes. Fourth, review app and device settings for the young person's accounts separately from adult accounts. Fifth, record each move with a date, so the handover has a visible history rather than happening all at once by accident.

title: Signature Research Consent Card
body:
The Signature Research Consent Card is an original design for carrying the essentials of a research consent on one card: what the consent covers, whether data is coded or identifiable, whether commercial use is allowed, whether results will be returned, and how withdrawal works and what it stops. The card is filled in from the full consent form before signing, and the signed card is kept with the study's contact details. Its purpose is to stop the common problem where a participant signs a long form and later cannot remember what was agreed, especially the limits of withdrawal.

Method. The working method for this record is a card filled before signing. First, read the full consent form. Second, copy the five essentials onto the card in plain words. Third, check the withdrawal limits carefully and write them exactly. Fourth, ask the study team about anything the card leaves blank. title: Signature Record Copy Desk
body:

When a record is wrong, the desk holds both the correction request and the reply, so the history of the correction is visible. title: Signature Telehealth Quiet Room
body:
The Signature Telehealth Quiet Room is an original design for a visit space that protects privacy by habit: a chosen corner, headphones, a closed door or a turned chair, and a pre-visit check that silences notifications and closes other apps. The room has a small sign for the household: a visit is in progress, please do not enter. After the visit, the room's closing habit is to sign out on shared devices and file the visit summary where it can be found. The design is deliberately low-tech, because privacy in a home visit depends more on household habits than on the platform's features.

Method. The working method for this record is a room routine in three parts. Before the visit, choose the space, test audio and video, and silence notifications. During the visit, confirm who is on the call and ask before anyone else joins. After the visit, sign out, review the summary, and file the instructions. If no private space is available, the routine includes asking to reschedule or to use a phone call from a safer place, rather than holding a sensitive visit where others can hear.

title: Signature Directive Envelope
body:
The Signature Directive Envelope is an original design for making advance directives findable in an emergency: a single envelope, clearly labeled, holding the directive and the names of the decision-maker, the primary clinician, and the hospital that holds a copy. The envelope's outside lists where copies live, without listing the directive's private details. The inside holds the document itself plus a one-page sheet stating who to call first. The envelope is stored where the decision-maker knows to look, and its location is told to family members, so a directive is found when it is needed rather than discovered afterwards.

Method. The working method for this record is an envelope chain. First, prepare the directive under the local rules that apply, such as witnesses. Second, place the original and the call sheet in the envelope. Third, give copies to the decision-maker, the clinician, and the hospital. Fourth, tell family members that the envelope exists and where it is, without sharing its private contents. Fifth, review the envelope after major life changes and after moving, because forms and rules differ by place.
